# The bake-off: six ways to make a decision {#sec-ch13}

::: {.epigraph by="C. A. R. Hoare, Turing Award lecture, 1980"}
There are two ways of constructing a software design: One way is to make it so simple that there are obviously no deficiencies, and the other way is to make it so complicated that there are no obvious deficiencies.
:::

Every team that makes decisions has the same never-ending argument. The senior expert says the hand-written rules are fine: you can read every one. The data scientist says a trained model would beat them, if someone labelled enough cases. The new engineer says an LLM reads cases better than both. And now someone has read about Jev.

Each is right about something; they're judging different things (explainability, accuracy, flexibility, price) and nobody puts all the numbers on one page. So let's: six methods, one dataset, one fair contest, every column that matters. Jev doesn't win every round.

::: {.goals}
- Compare rules, logistic regression, a trained text classifier, LLM structured output, LLM-as-judge and Jev on the same decision.
- Score them on ranking, calibration, labels needed, speed, price and stability, not on one number.
- See where Jev loses, and why that's useful to know.
- Pick a method, or a combination, from a scorecard.
:::

## The contestants

The decision: is this alert a real threat? Every method gets the three history weeks to train or tune on: {{< num ch20 n_hist int >}} alerts with analysts' verdicts. Then every method is scored on the fourth week, the "live week": {{< num ch20 n_live int >}} alerts it has never seen, of which {{< num ch20 live_threats int >}} are real.

![The six contestants: what each one reads, what it returns, and what it needs before it can start.](/figures/ch20/contenders.pdf){#fig-contenders}

Each reads what it would read in practice (@fig-contenders). Rules and logistic regression get the alert's structured fields. The **text classifier**, a simple word-counting model trained on the labels (a stand-in for a fine-tuned model, which would usually do better), and both LLM methods get the raw text. Jev gets the fields as structured input.

The most important paragraph in this chapter: both LLM contestants are the book's stand-in, built to read alerts *less accurately* than the Jev stand-in. So when the LLM ranks worse than Jev below, that's how the stand-ins were made, not evidence about real models. What you *can* rely on is the rest: how stated confidences behave, how often free-text JSON breaks, what asking twice does, and what labels cost. Those come from how each *kind* of method works.

## Round one: ranking

The first question is the one people usually ask: which method puts the real threats at the top?

![Three views of how well each method separates threats from harmless alerts, on the live week. Left: ranking quality (AUC). Middle: the share of all real threats found if the team reviews the top 240 alerts each day. Right: calibration error, where lower is better.](/figures/ch20/scores.pdf){#fig-scores}

Logistic regression wins round one, by a small margin: an AUC of {{< num ch20 logistic_auc f3 >}} against Jev's {{< num ch20 jev_auc f3 >}} (@fig-scores). With a review capacity of 240 alerts a day, it catches {{< num ch20 logistic_caught pct >}} of real threats; Jev catches {{< num ch20 jev_caught pct >}}.

That isn't luck. It was trained on fifteen thousand of this company's own labelled alerts, on clean fields, for a decision that depends on them almost in a straight line. That's classic machine learning's home ground. A general model with no training on this company shouldn't be expected to beat it there.

The rules come last on ranking, with an AUC of {{< num ch20 rules_auc f2 >}}. The reason is simple: a rule only says yes or no. Among the hundreds of alerts it says yes to, it has no way to say which to look at first.

Give Jev the raw text instead of the fields, and its AUC drops to {{< num ch20 jev_text_auc f3 >}}. That's still well ahead of the trained text classifier's {{< num ch20 text_clf_auc f3 >}}. A classifier that counts words is worst at reading "threat intel score: 0.82" as a number.

## Round two: calibration

Ranking is half the job; thresholds need probabilities that mean what they say.

![Reliability diagrams for each method on the live week. On the dashed line, what a method said matches what happened. Most methods here are close. The LLM's stated confidences are grouped on a few values; the judge's ratings, read as probabilities, are far too high in the middle.](/figures/ch20/reliability.pdf){#fig-reliability}

Most contestants sit near the diagonal (@fig-reliability). The two LLM methods are the interesting ones. The LLM's *written* confidence used only {{< num ch20 conf_levels int >}} different values across five thousand alerts, mostly 0.9, 0.95 and 0.99: a number a model *writes* is text, and text likes round numbers. So it can't rank finely. And the **LLM-as-judge**, rating each alert 1 to 10, gives the worst calibration in the contest ({{< num ch20 llm_judge_ece f3 >}}) when its rating is read as a probability. Platt scaling on a few hundred labels would fix it, but then it's no longer a method that needs zero labels.

## Round three: how many labels?

"Logistic regression wins" comes at a cost: fifteen thousand labels. What if you have fewer?

![Ranking on the live week as the trained methods see more labelled alerts, averaged over random samples. Jev and the LLMs need no labels to start, so they're flat lines. Logistic regression catches up with Jev at about 3,000 labels.](/figures/ch20/labels.pdf){#fig-labels}

@fig-labels is the chart for the data scientist. Logistic regression needs about 3,000 labelled cases to catch up with Jev; with a few hundred it's clearly behind. A mature team with months of history has that. A new team, or a brand-new decision nobody has labelled, doesn't. (The word-counting classifier never catches up: counting words misses the numbers in the text.)

::: {.keyidea}
Labels are the hidden cost of trained models: a method that needs none can start today.
:::

A method that needs thousands has to wait for them, and needs them again when things change.

## Round four: speed and price

![Time and cost per decision for each method, on log scales. Classic models run in millionths of a second, for fractions of a cent per million decisions (an assumption: computing cost only). The LLM figures are this book's illustrative assumptions; Jev's are vendor-reported.](/figures/ch20/cost-latency.pdf){#fig-cost-latency}

Nothing beats a rule on speed or price, and classic models are close behind: millionths of a second, on computers you already own (@fig-cost-latency). Jev's vendor-reported figures sit in between: about \${{< num ch20 jev_cost_m int >}} per million decisions, tens to hundreds of milliseconds. The illustrative LLM: about \${{< num ch20 llm_json_cost_m int >}} per million and {{< num ch20 llm_json_latency f1 >}} seconds.

::: {.keyidea}
If a rule or a logistic regression can make a decision well, use one of them.
:::

It's cheaper and faster by a factor of a thousand or more. Jev's price advantage is against *LLMs*, not against everything.

## Round five: the same answer twice

![Left: the share of alerts whose verdict changed across five identical calls. Right: the share of answers that couldn't be parsed at all.](/figures/ch20/variance.pdf){#fig-variance-13}

Ask the LLM the same question five times at a temperature of 0.7, and {{< num ch20 flip_rate pct1 >}} of verdicts change at least once (@fig-variance-13). At temperature 0 answers mostly repeat, though not always with real APIs. And {{< num ch20 parse_fail pct1 >}} of its JSON answers couldn't be parsed at all; in a real system, each is an error your code must handle. Typed answers can't fail to parse: the probabilities arrive as numbers in a fixed shape.

## The scorecard

::: {.wide}
![The whole contest on one page. Bold marks the best in each numeric column. Every accuracy number is synthetic; every cost and time is an assumption, an illustration, or vendor-reported, as marked.](/figures/ch20/scorecard.pdf){#fig-scorecard-13}
:::

Read @fig-scorecard-13 by column, not by row, and ask which columns *your* decision cares about.

If you have thousands of labels, clean fields and a decision that doesn't change much, logistic regression is hard to beat. It ranks best, it's calibrated, it's nearly free, and you can read its weights. Jev clearly loses there.

If you need to explain every decision to an auditor, rules clearly win the last column, and nothing else comes close.

If you have no labels, raw text, or many different decisions to make, Jev's row is the strongest. It starts with zero labels and ranks nearly as well as the trained model. After a calibration check, you can put thresholds on its probabilities. Its answers come in a shape that can't break, and it costs a small fraction of an LLM call.

And the LLM? Weakest at deciding here, partly by construction. But it does what no other row tries: it reads anything, and it *writes*. That's why Chapter 15's first pattern gives it extracting and explaining, and gives the decision to something else.

::: {.breaks}
One decision, one synthetic company, stand-ins for the LLM and for Jev; the gap between those two was built in. One live week has only about four hundred real threats, so second-decimal differences in AUC could be chance. The value of a bake-off is the *method*: run the same contest on your own data, with the real models.
:::

::: {.threshold}
A new team is taking over cloud-storage alerts, a decision nobody has labelled. They'll get about 300 labels a week from their own reviews. Which method would you start with, and when would you think about switching? What would you use the first 300 labels for?

(Start with a method that needs no labels, Jev in this contest. Use the first 300 labels to check and fix its calibration, as in Chapter 11. After three or four weeks of labels, train a logistic regression next to it and compare them on the next week. If the two agree closely, keep the cheaper one. If they disagree, look at the alerts where they disagree.)
:::

There's even a theorem behind this, for optimisation [@wolpert1997], and it fits any bake-off:

::: {.keyidea}
There is no best method, only a best method for a particular decision.
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. If you Platt-scale the LLM-as-judge ratings on 300 labelled alerts, what happens to its ECE? To its AUC? Why does one change and not the other?
2. Build a scorecard for a decision in your own work. Which three columns matter most? Which method would you try first?
:::

:::
